rejected.title: Barriers in plants
card: Plants have no skin or mucus. Their first defence is a set of barriers on the outside that stop pathogens getting in. These barriers work against many kinds of pathogen, not one type.
Physical
a waxy cuticle covers the leaf surface and repels water, which makes it hard for pathogens to stick. Thick cell walls, and bark on woody stems, form a tough layer that is hard to break through.
Chemical
plants make chemicals that harm pathogens, such as antimicrobial compounds and toxins. Some are always present and some are made after an attack starts.
Pathogens can still get past these barriers through wounds or through the small pores in leaves. This is why plants rely on both barriers and chemicals.
rejected.remember: Plants block pathogens with tough outer layers and harm them with chemicals.

a.q: A fungal spore lands on a leaf but cannot stick, and it is washed off before it grows. Which defence stopped it?
opts: The waxy cuticle on the leaf surface
The thick cell walls inside the leaf
Chemicals the leaf makes after an attack
The bark that covers the woody stem
a.why: The waxy cuticle repels water, so the spore cannot stick to the surface. Thick cell walls are tempting, but they resist being broken through, and the spore never got that far. No attack started, so chemicals made after an attack were not involved.
a.clue: The spore never got inside the leaf.

b.q: A fungus lands on a tree in Gippsland and cannot get into the trunk, but it enters through a deep crack where a branch has broken off. What does this show?
opts: A wound gives pathogens a way past the outer layer
The tree's chemicals do not work against any fungi
Cell walls block bacteria but never block fungi
The tree has no defence once a pathogen gets in
b.why: Bark and thick cell walls blocked the fungus on the intact trunk. The broken branch left a wound, which gave the fungus a way past that layer. It is wrong to say the tree has no defence once the fungus is in, because plants can make chemicals after an attack starts.
b.clue: What did the broken branch change about the outer layer?

a.q: Which feature of a leaf helps stop a fungal pathogen from sticking to its surface?
opts: A waxy cuticle that repels water
A layer of mucus that traps spores
Stomach acid that kills microbes
Skin cells that are shed often
a.why: The waxy cuticle repels water and makes the surface hard for pathogens to stick to. Mucus is a barrier in animals, not in plants, so it is not the answer, even though it also traps pathogens.
a.clue: Plants have no mucus, skin or stomach.

b.q: A fungus lands on a tree in Gippsland and cannot get into the trunk, but it enters through a deep crack where a branch has broken off. What does this show?
opts: The tough outer layer works only while it is unbroken
The tree's chemicals do not work against fungi
Cell walls are only a barrier to bacteria
The tree has no defence once a pathogen lands
b.why: Bark and thick cell walls block pathogens while they are intact. A wound removes that barrier and gives the fungus a way in. The tree still has chemical defences, so it is wrong to say it has no defence.
b.clue: What did the broken branch change about the outer layer?

a.best: A waxy cuticle that repels water

b.best: The tough outer layer works only while it is unbroken

problems.detail: The clue 'Plants have no mucus, skin or stomach' rules out all three distractors at once, which hands the student the answer without testing the idea.
All three distractors are animal features, so the only plant feature stands out. This is too easy for Year 12.

The right option says the outer layer 'works only while it is unbroken', but the card says only that pathogens 'can' get past through wounds or leaf pores. Even an unbroken surface has openings (stomata), so the absolute 'only' overstates the card.
